section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: This chapter began with one small calculation:

The forbidden value h=0 did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. That idea became the language of limits. Limits then gave us continuity, one-sided behavior, infinite behavior, asymptotes, sequences, and two existence theorems.
Before we use limits to define derivatives, it is worth pausing to see the whole map.

subsection.title: The chapter in one picture
subsection.p: A limit is the central idea. The other ideas in the chapter are different ways of asking what a limit is doing.

figure.caption: Limits are the center. Continuity, asymptotes, sequences, and tangent slopes all use the same idea of controlled approach.

subsection.p: The most important habit is not memorizing a table of limit forms. It is asking:
subsection.md: \text{What is the input doing, and what target is the output approaching?}

exercise.title: What one idea sits at the center of the chapter?

statement.p: The chapter began with a forbidden value h=0 that did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. In your own words, what does a limit watch, and why can continuity, one-sided behavior, asymptotes, and sequences all be seen as different ways of asking the same nearby-target question?

hint.p: A limit is a controlled approach to a target. Sometimes the input is a real number, sometimes a whole-number index, sometimes only one side, and sometimes the target is infinite rather than finite.

subsection.title: A decision guide for limits and continuity
subsection.p: When you face a limit problem, begin with the simplest test. Then move only as far as the problem requires.

Use continuity or the limit laws.
Factor, cancel, expand, combine fractions, or rationalize. Then try again.
left and right sides behave differently
Compute one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists only if they agree.
Check signs from the left and right. The limit may be \infty, -\infty, or may fail to exist.
Divide by the largest power, or compare leading terms.
an oscillating factor is multiplied by something small
a theorem about continuous functions is tempting
Check the hypotheses first: continuity, closed interval, bounded interval, and the right endpoint information.
Use the \varepsilon-N definition, algebraic limit laws, or monotone bounded convergence.

subsection.p: The warning examples in Section should stay close by. Most mistakes come from using a true theorem without checking the conditions that make it true.

exercise.title: What should you check before forcing a two-sided finite limit?

statement.p: Direct substitution, the form \frac00, disagreeing sides, and unbounded growth are different pictures. In your own words, how do you decide whether to substitute, rewrite, split into one-sided limits, or refuse a finite two-sided claim?

hint.p: A number from substitution is the calm case. The form \frac00 is a question. Different one-sided stories block a two-sided limit. Growth without bound is infinite behavior, not a real-number target.

exercise.title: Why do IVT and EVT mistakes usually come from missing hypotheses?

statement.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem guarantee that answers exist; they do not usually compute those answers. In your own words, which hypotheses must be checked before using each theorem, and why is a true theorem still illegal to apply when a condition is missing?

hint.p: IVT needs continuity on a closed interval. EVT needs continuity on a closed and bounded interval. The warning examples show what breaks if you skip those conditions.

subsection.title: End-of-chapter hook
subsection.p: A limit watches a quantity approach a target. In this chapter, the quantity might have been a function value, a sequence term, or an average velocity.
The next chapter chooses one limit and builds a new object from it:
The numerator measures change in output. The denominator measures change in input. The quotient is an average rate of change. The limit, if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change.
That number is the derivative.

exercise.title: What new object is the next chapter about to build from a limit?

statement.p: The next chapter chooses the limit \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}. In your own words, what do the numerator and denominator measure, why is the quotient still an average, and what extra meaning appears if that limit exists?

hint.p: The numerator is change in output. The denominator is change in input. The quotient is an average rate. The limit, if it exists, is the instantaneous rate: the derivative.
